title: "Go, you are free"
hook: he forgives the people who drove him out, echoing Yusuf, no blame on you today (12:92)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Sufyan's city, Mecca, conquered: ten thousand at his back, and the Prophet ﷺ riding in with his head bowed so low his beard nearly touched the saddle. Your line was head bowed on the camel. Did you walk into a room a little more quietly? Day two hundred seventy-eight.

The square around the Ka'ba is full that day, and the faces are familiar. Some of these people had mocked him in the street for years. Some had boycotted his clan, shutting them up hungry in a narrow valley, chased him out of his hometown, and fought him at Badr and Uhud. One of the women in that crowd had rejoiced over the body of his uncle Hamzah. Now the city is his. There's no army left to stop him. The early biographies say he turned to them and asked a question: what do you think I'm going to do to you? And they answered carefully, the way you answer when your life depends on it: good. You're a noble brother, the son of a noble brother. Today, what he said next.
screen: `THE PEOPLE WHO DROVE HIM OUT.` → `WHAT DO YOU THINK I'LL DO?` → `GOOD, NOBLE BROTHER.`

segments.voice: According to the early accounts of his life, he said: I say to you what Yusuf said to his brothers. No blame on you today. Go, you are free. Hold on to that first sentence, because he didn't make up a speech. He reached for a story everyone listening knew. In the Qur'an's twelfth surah, Joseph's brothers throw him into a well, and he is sold away. Years later they stand in front of him in Egypt, hungry, not knowing who he is, and when they finally realize, they're ashamed. And Yusuf says, in the Qur'an's words, that there is no blame on them this day, and that God will forgive them. The Prophet stepped into that story on purpose. He was saying: you're my brothers, and I'm doing what Yusuf did. The word the reports use for the people of Mecca after this is tulaqa', the freed ones. The ones who were let go. Notice what forgiveness here is not. It isn't pretending nothing happened. Everyone in that square knew exactly what had happened; that's why they were afraid. It isn't weakness either. He could have done anything. It's choosing, from a position of strength, not to collect the debt. Some of the people let go that day became Muslims, and some later became leaders of the community. Muslim teachers often point out that he wasn't only forgiving strangers. Some of these people were his own relatives. Family is often the hardest place to say: go, you're free.
screen: `WHAT YUSUF SAID TO HIS BROTHERS.` · `NO BLAME ON YOU TODAY.` · `TULAQA' — THE FREED ONES.` · `FORGIVING FROM STRENGTH.` · then, large: `GO, YOU ARE FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive an old enemy in your heart. Sit, and let your breath slow. Think of someone who hurt you a long time ago. Not the worst thing that ever happened to you; something you've been carrying for a while. You don't have to call them. You don't have to say it was fine. Just picture them for a moment, and see if you can let the debt go, even a little. If you pray, you can ask God to forgive them, and you. If you don't, just try the words quietly: go, you're free. The bell holds the time.
Go. The first word of what he told the people who'd driven him out: go, you are free. Today's word.

Your line: no blame on you today. Today, when an old grudge surfaces, in traffic, at a family dinner, scrolling past a name, say the line once to yourself and see what it loosens. Day two hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the forgiveness at the conquest of Mecca as a model of mercy, and many teachers use it, together with Yusuf's words to his brothers, when urging people to forgive relatives and old enemies.

fork.setup: you're the Prophet ﷺ. the city that drove you out is yours, and the people who fought you stand waiting. what do you do?
options: punish the leaders as a warning.
say what Yusuf said: no blame on you today. go, you are free.
leave the city to them and go home to Medina.
fork.reveal: the early biographies say he quoted Yusuf and let them go. the people of Mecca were called the tulaqa', the freed ones.

original.note: Arabic: the freed ones, the name given to the people of Mecca let go that day.

trapdoor: what you thought: a victor being generous.
what it means: forgiving from strength, the debt fully known and not collected, even from family.
what a scholar hears: he frames it as Yusuf's words to his brothers (12:92), turning the conquest into a family reunion; the people of Mecca became the tulaqa'.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: removed 'some had thrown filth on him while he prayed' (Bukhari 240 says the men behind that were killed at Badr, so they were not in the crowd) and the unsourced 'three years'; hook no longer opens 'Picture'; the teach wrongly called tulaqa' 'our word today' (the word is 'Go'), cut; Yusuf's brothers 'ashamed' (12:91), not 'terrified'; 'many became Muslims' softened in teach and myth.

The 'go, you are free' (idhhabu fa-antum at-tulaqa') report is from Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham and later collections (e.g. al-Bayhaqi); hadith scholars have questioned its chain. The script says 'according to the early accounts'. Confirm this framing.
The woman who rejoiced over Hamzah's body (Hind bint Utbah) is alluded to without naming her; she accepted Islam at the conquest. Confirm the allusion is appropriate.
'Some had thrown filth on him while he prayed' refers to the camel-entrails incident (Sahih al-Bukhari 240); confirm.
The word for this day is the index's title head, '"Go'; the word screen shows the whole phrase. The owner may want a cleaner index word (e.g. tulaqa').
12:92 paraphrased rather than quoted from Pickthall; a Keeper may wish to add the Pickthall wording.
